replies.author: bunnyUFO

The way I would phrase this is:
You are the Director/CEO. Fable is middle management verifying everything is right and on track. Opus is team lead, sometimes develops, plans, or leads other staff. Sonnet and Haiku do most deployment and busy work.

replies.author: bunnyUFO
replies.body:
I default to medium on all of them. If given a clear plan with context on design and development details sonnet is enough for most small-mid sized tasks (though this is subjective). 

Just spend more time planning and chatting with opus and downstairs sonnet tasks/sessions will be very capable and cost less. If each task is a new session it also manages context effectively.

Haiku is more for quick easy changes or things you would except someone with less context to do like qualitative feedback output. Having it use your app (without access to code, html, css, DOM, JavaScript) and reporting bugs or how it "felt" to use.

You want opus to design game systems and sonnet to develop them. Haiku van make small changes to existing well documented features or be used as dumber qualitative QA. Fable can be more for figuring out what festurs/systems you even need in the first place for the kind of game/app you are making. The. Verifying those desires are right after implementation.

comments.author: SilliCarl

I cant say for sure, but I've used Opus 5.5 for 90% of my project, then I've come up with a list of problems that Opus is struggling to solve, I'm currently giving those to Fable in hopes that it is able to unlock that final 10% for me.

Namely I'm trying to get it to work out enemy AI, which is an absolute knot of problems.

replies.author: Adorable_Sandwich_48
replies.body: What kind of approach you used for your AI?

replies.author: SilliCarl
replies.body:
For enemy AI? 

My game is a grand strategy game where you balance economy, combat & diplomacy. There are 99 AI controllers in a round and so the enemy AI is incredibly complex.   
At a very base level it uses a point system to decide what actions to take and what actions not to take.  
Those points are then modified by contextual information. 

At a very base level say "attack this location" has a point score of 1 and "make peace with x" has a point score of 2

The AI will try to make peace.   
but maybe the AI's personality is aggressive. Maybe that gives a 3x multiplier to any "attack" coded actions.   
Thus "attack this location" becomes 3 points and make peace is still 2. so it attacks. 

each AI has 8 personality sliders that all manipulate and change the base points in various ways so that each of the 99 AI make a slightly different choice than any other. essentially if you give the same starting position to each AI, over the course of a round it'll end with a wildly different outcome. 

AI controllers are further manipulated with an "intelligence" system, essentially you have 6 stages of "intelligence" and depending on the level, the AI will act in more or less reasonable ways. A really dumb AI might suicide into you because it mis-judged the fight, where the highest tier AI might manipulate and deceive you into launching bad attacks, it might make false attacks on one location then strike at another, it might engage in diplomacy for the express purpose of tricking you. it will look for more information on your forces before comiting to a game changing fight. 

As you can probably tell from this ramble, its very complex. I've been working on it  (just the AI) for legit 2-3 months now. I've been working on the game for 5 months total (ish).

replies.author: Adorable_Sandwich_48
replies.body: I mean I don't think you didn't, but try to ask opus to look at the best open source examples of the games that have similar problems solved or maybe even just at some generic information about how it was done in different games if such information is available. It can open up a lot. Was struggling for ai In my game, I really didn't have any experience and only thinga I knew were behavioral trees or utility ai. So my abstract task didn't end well, a few weeks of work produced almost 0 result. But then I asked it to look at the best or good AIs in class like quake 3, half life some other games and that allowed to finally get something manageable and scalable that works pretty decent.

replies.author: SilliCarl
replies.body: Thanks for the advice! I appreciate it!

replies.author: SimCFB
replies.body:
You probably already figured this out but an approach like this requires a gigantic amount of iteration with very well defined goals. 

I had a similar process for [www.simcfb.com](http://www.simcfb.com)

Instead of enemy factions I was simulating player behavior. Also quite complex when you get into the weeds. How a player behaves in this formation is different from another. 

I wasted like 5 weeks trying to make it neural. Burnt through like $200 worth of GCP credits doing all sorts of pytorch tests. Ultimately went for simpler alogrithms. Still very complex but not as complicated as real neural nets playing the game. 

So I dunno maybe if the results are well defined the neural approach is something you could play around with. That would make the enemy AI literally unpredictable.
